1.tHtml:
Receptionist: Good morning, Lakeside Hotel Reservations. How can I help you today?
Caller: Good morning. I'd like to enquire about booking a room for myself and my wife. We're planning to arrive on the twelfth of May.1
Receptionist: Certainly. Let me take some details. May I have your name, please?
Caller: Yes, it's Andrew Brennan. That's B-R-E-N-N-A-N.
Receptionist: Thank you, Mr Brennan. And how many nights are you planning to stay?
Caller: We'd like to stay for three nights, so from the twelfth until the fifteenth of May.3
Receptionist: I see. We have a double room available at ninety-five pounds per night.4 That includes breakfast. Would that suit you?
Caller: Yes, that sounds fine. Could you also tell me what time we can check in?
Receptionist: Check-in is from two o'clock in the afternoon onwards.6 Is there anything else you need?
Caller: Actually, yes. My wife uses a wheelchair, so we'd need a room on the ground floor if possible.
Receptionist: I understand. We do have accessible rooms available. I'll make a note of that requirement. Would you like us to provide any special equipment?
Caller: A shower seat would be very helpful, thank you.8
Receptionist: Not a problem. That can be arranged at no extra charge. Shall I go ahead and confirm the booking with your credit card details?
Caller: Yes, please. The card number is oh-four-seven-one, five-five-two-two, one-one-eight-eight, six-seven-four-three.9
Receptionist: Thank you. I've processed the payment. Your confirmation number is seven-seven-two-four.10 Is there anything else?
Caller: No, that's everything. Thank you for your help.
Receptionist: You're welcome, Mr Brennan. We look forward to seeing you on the twelfth. Goodbye.
Caller: Goodbye.

2.tHtml: Workshop Coordinator: Welcome to Bridge Street Cycle Workshop. My name is Harriet, and11 I will be looking after the Saturday morning group12. Before we start, let me give you a quick tour of the main room so you know where everything lives. Coming through the double doors, the first thing on your left is the row of workbenches17. Each bench seats two riders, and every bench has its own small set of Allen keys in a red tray. On the right-hand wall, just past the front window, we have the parts library18, a tall wooden shelving unit with labelled drawers for brake blocks, cables, inner tubes, and similar small items. If you carry on along the same wall, you will find the cleaning station, with a sink, a brush rack, and a stack of blue cotton cloths for drying frames after washing. At the back of the room, behind the central rack, there is the diagnostic area, with a truing stand, a spoke tension meter, and a small laptop used to log wheel and gear measurements. A few practical notes before you begin. Sessions run from half past nine13 until twelve thirty, and we close for a short tea break at quarter past eleven14. Please wear closed-toe shoes and bring your own water bottle. The shop next door sells snacks, but it is not part of the workshop. The cost for a Saturday block is fifteen pounds,15 payable by card at the front desk before the first session, or in cash on the day to me directly. If you need a spare part during a session, write the part name and your name on a slip from the yellow pad by the parts library,16 then hand the slip to one of the volunteer mechanics. Tools stay in the workshop. Bikes and personal bags should go in the cage near the back door, as the floor must stay clear for safety. Right, that is the room. We will start the morning with a ten-minute talk on basic brake checks, then move to the workbenches.

3.tHtml:
Harriet: So, how are you feeling about the research project now that the supervisor's gone through our draft sections?
Luca: Honestly, a bit mixed. I thought the methods section was the strongest, but I've had second thoughts after her comments22.
Harriet: Really? I felt the opposite. I thought the literature review was the part that needed the most work.
Luca: Maybe. She was quite firm that we should not be leaning so heavily on the older sources, and that did pull the literature review down a bit.
Harriet: And I suppose the discussion section was where she had the most detailed notes, wasn't it.
Luca: Definitely. She said the strongest part of the discussion was23 the way we'd framed the main argument. That came through clearly in her notes.
Harriet: So the discussion is what she's most happy with overall, even though there's plenty to revise.
Luca: On the results section, she seemed happier than I'd expected, actually. I'd assumed she'd push for more statistical detail, but she was fine with how we'd presented the figures.
Harriet: What about the conclusion? I wasn't sure whether she'd see it as rushed.
Luca: She wasn't harsh on it, but she did flag that the limitations paragraph felt under-developed25 compared with the rest of the section.
Harriet: And the abstract? She barely mentioned it.
Luca: She said the abstract was acceptable as it stood, with no major issues26, which surprised me a bit. I'd expected more comments there.
Harriet: Looking back, do you think the methods section is what she'd most want us to improve?
Luca: Not the methods, I think. The methods was the strongest part for her too, on the whole. The clearest thing from her notes was that the literature review is the area to focus on next29.
Harriet: And in terms of what kind of action she wants, she didn't actually tell us to scrap anything and start again, did she?
Luca: No, she didn't ask us to rewrite any of the sections from scratch. The next step is to revise what we have, keeping the overall structure, and address her specific points one by one.
Harriet: That sounds manageable. And the reference list, she didn't flag that either?
Luca: She thought the reference list was the most accurate part of the whole draft. The citation style was consistent throughout, she said, and the dates all matched the sources.
Harriet: So our next supervision meeting, when is it booked for?
Luca: Tuesday the eleventh of March, in her office, at half past two in the afternoon. I'll put it in the shared calendar once we hang up.

4.tHtml: Lecturer: Good morning, everyone. Today's session focuses on professional development for newly qualified teachers31 joining secondary schools. We will begin with the induction programme, which runs across the first two terms32 and includes four observed teaching practice sessions. Each new teacher is paired with a mentor who observes lessons every fortnight and provides a written report at the end of each half term. Mentors are usually drawn from the same subject department33, and they hold at least five years34 of classroom experience. The mentor's first priority is to help the new teacher manage workload35, particularly marking and lesson preparation during the autumn term. Alongside mentoring, the school runs a series of optional workshops, held on Wednesday afternoons36, covering behaviour management, assessment design and the use of digital tools in the classroom. Teachers who complete at least three workshops37 receive a certificate, and a small allowance of two hundred pounds to spend38 on classroom resources. All new teachers are expected to join the peer observation group, which meets in the main staffroom on the first Monday of each month. At the end of the year, each teacher submits a reflective portfolio containing two lesson plans, samples of student work and a short action research report. The portfolio is reviewed by the head of department and the deputy headteacher40, and successful candidates progress to the main professional development track. If you have any questions, please come and see me after the session. Office hours are posted on the staff noticeboard each week.

Receptionist: Good afternoon, Riverside Hotel, how can I help you?
Caller: Good afternoon. I'm calling about the booking I made online last week. I'd like to check a few details please.
Receptionist: Of course, I'd be happy to help. May I have your surname and booking reference number?
Caller: Yes, it's Thompson, and the reference is RH7842.2
Receptionist: Thank you, Mrs Thompson. I can see your booking here. You're booked for two nights, starting on the fifteenth of June, arriving on the Saturday evening.3
Caller: That's right. I was wondering if we could check the room type. We booked a double room, but my colleague mentioned we might have been upgraded.
Receptionist: Let me see... Yes, we've been able to upgrade you to a deluxe double with a river view on the third floor.5
Caller: Oh, that's lovely, thank you. What time is check-in on the Saturday?
Receptionist: Check-in is from two o'clock in the afternoon. However, if you arrive earlier, you're welcome to leave your luggage at reception.
Caller: Great. And could you tell me if breakfast is included with that room?
Receptionist: Yes, a full English breakfast is included each morning, served in the dining room from seven until ten.6
Caller: Perfect. One more question, do you have secure parking at the hotel?
Receptionist: We do. We have an underground car park with CCTV coverage. The charge is eight pounds per night.7
Caller: That's fine. Is it possible to pay for the parking when we check out rather than when we arrive?
Receptionist: Absolutely, you can settle that along with any extras when you check out.8 Will there be anything else?
Caller: Yes, I need to let you know we'll be checking in quite late, around eleven thirty on the Saturday night.9 Will there still be someone at the desk?
Receptionist: Yes, our reception is staffed twenty-four hours, so that won't be a problem at all.10
Caller: Excellent. I think that covers everything. Thank you very much for your help.
Receptionist: You're welcome, Mrs Thompson. We look forward to welcoming you on the fifteenth. Goodbye.
Caller: Goodbye.

Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Heritage Museum. My name is Sarah and I'll be your guide this afternoon. Before we begin the tour, I'd like to share some important information about your visit and introduce you to what you'll discover here.
The museum is open seven days a week, including public holidays, from ten in the morning until six in the evening. We're closed only on Christmas Day11. Entry to the permanent galleries is completely free12, which means you can explore our main exhibitions at no cost. However, we do charge for the temporary exhibitions in the east wing and for the special interactive displays on the second floor.
Regarding refreshments, our café is located on the ground floor13 at the end of the main corridor, and it serves hot and cold drinks along with a selection of sandwiches and cakes. The café opens at half past ten and closes at five14. For those interested in souvenirs or books, our shop is on the left as you enter through the main doors15, and it stays open until ten minutes before the museum closes.
Now, let me tell you about the layout of the museum. As you walk through the entrance, you'll find the reception desk directly ahead. To your left is the temporary exhibition space, which currently features a fascinating display about local industry in the nineteenth century16. Straight ahead and to the right is our permanent River Valley Gallery, which chronicles the history of the river and its significance to the development of our town. This gallery is particularly popular with visitors, so I'd recommend visiting it first if you can.
The museum also offers a range of activities for families and children. Our workshop room, which is on the upper ground floor17, hosts craft sessions every Saturday and Sunday at eleven and at two o'clock. These sessions are included in the general entry price, though we do ask that you book a place in advance because they tend to fill up quickly. The workshop sessions focus on different themes each week, and this weekend's theme is traditional boat-building18, which ties in nicely with our river theme.
Finally, I'd like to mention our guided tours. These run twice daily, at eleven in the morning and again at three in the afternoon. The morning tour focuses on the industrial history of the region, while the afternoon tour covers the cultural and artistic heritage. Tours last approximately ninety minutes19 and depart from the reception desk. There's no need to book the morning tour, but afternoon tours must be reserved at least one day in advance20.
Are there any questions before we begin?

Maya: Hi David, have you got a minute? I wanted to go over our presentation plan before our tutorial with Professor Chen tomorrow.
David: Sure Maya, come in. I've been looking at the feedback from the last seminar. It was quite useful actually.
Maya: Yes, I thought so too. She said we need to be clearer about our methodology. I've been working on that section of the draft.
David: Good. I have also added some more recent case studies on urban recycling programmes.21 There is a really interesting one from Amsterdam that I found.23
Maya: That sounds perfect. We need to strengthen the practical applications part. The theory is there but we should show how it works in real cities.
David: Exactly. I also think we should mention the challenges we faced with data collection. Professor Chen always says that demonstrates critical thinking.
Maya: Agreed. I have to be honest though, the interviews were harder than I expected. Some participants were quite reluctant to discuss their waste management habits.22
David: That is a common problem in social research. We should include a note about that in the methodology section. It will make our analysis more transparent.
Maya: I will draft a paragraph explaining the ethical considerations. We need to make sure we cover that before we submit.
David: I will also look at the literature review again. I found some newer articles on circular economy models that we could reference.
Maya: Brilliant. We should also think about the visual aids. Professor Chen mentioned that presentations with clear data visualisations tend to score higher.24
David: I have started working on some charts. I thought a comparison between three cities would work well. Perhaps Amsterdam, Singapore and Cape Town.29
Maya: That is a good spread. Different economic contexts and different approaches. It will make our argument more robust.
David: Should we meet before the tutorial tomorrow? I could come to the library at ten if that suits you.
Maya: Yes, that works for me. I will bring my laptop so we can review everything together.
David: Perfect. Oh, and did you see Professor Chen's message about the deadline? She has extended it by one week.25
Maya: I saw that. It is helpful but I would rather not leave it too late. We still need to incorporate the peer review feedback too.
David: True. I will send you my updated draft by Wednesday evening.26 You can add your sections and we can review it on Thursday.
Maya: Sounds like a plan. I will also check if there are any upcoming guest lectures on sustainable urban design. They might give us some additional perspectives.
David: Good idea. Right, I should get back to my literature search. See you at ten tomorrow.
Maya: See you then. And thanks for the help with the methodology section.
David: No problem. We are a team after all.
Maya: (Prof Chen joins) Oh Professor Chen, we were just discussing our presentation. We have incorporated your feedback and we are ready for tomorrow's tutorial.
Prof Chen: Excellent. I look forward to seeing your progress. Please remember that the visual presentation is worth fifteen percent of the overall marks.27
Maya: We have prepared some charts and diagrams. David has found some excellent case studies.
Prof Chen: Good. And do not forget to practise your timing. The presentation should be no longer than twelve minutes.28
David: We have timed it already. It comes to about eleven minutes with questions at the end.
Prof Chen: Perfect. I am pleased that you are on schedule. Any final questions before tomorrow?
Maya: Just one. Should we prepare printed handouts for the tutorial or is a digital version sufficient?
Prof Chen: Digital is fine. Just make sure everyone in the group has a copy on their device.30 And bring your notes in case we go into detailed discussion.
David: Thank you Professor. We will see you tomorrow at two.
Prof Chen: Yes, see you then. Good luck with your final preparations.

4.tHtml: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to discuss a phenomenon that's increasingly concerning marine biologists: ocean acidification and its effects on coral reef ecosystems. Now, let me start by explaining what ocean acidification actually means. Put simply, it's a reduction in the pH of the Earth's oceans, caused primarily by the absorption of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere31. Since the industrial revolution, the ocean has absorbed approximately 30 percent of all human-generated carbon emissions. This might sound like a good thing for the atmosphere, but it has serious consequences for marine life. The key problem lies in chemistry. When CO2 dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid. This acid releases hydrogen ions, which increase the ocean's acidity. Over the past 200 years, the average pH of ocean surface waters has dropped from 8.2 to 8.1. While this might seem like a minor change, it represents roughly a 26 percent increase in acidity. Now, why are coral reefs so vulnerable to these changes? Well, corals build their skeletons through a process called calcification33, which requires calcium carbonate. In more acidic waters, the chemical平衡 necessary for calcification is disrupted. The hydrogen ions essentially compete with the calcium ions, making it harder for corals to build and maintain their skeletons. This process is often compared to osteoporosis in humans34, where the structure becomes weaker over time. Beyond corals themselves, ocean acidification affects numerous other marine organisms. Shellfish, for example, including oysters and mussels, also rely on calcium carbonate to build their shells. Studies have shown that juvenile oysters in acidic conditions have significantly higher mortality rates. Similarly, certain species of plankton called pteropods35, which form a crucial part of the marine food web, are already showing shell dissolution in naturally acidic waters. This is particularly concerning because pteropods are a primary food source for many fish species, including salmon. The economic implications are substantial too. Coral reefs support approximately 500 million people worldwide36 and contribute roughly 375 billion dollars to the global economy37 through tourism, fisheries and coastal protection. If reef ecosystems continue to decline, we can expect significant impacts on food security and livelihoods. Now, some researchers are exploring whether marine organisms might adapt to these changing conditions over time. Studies on certain seaweed species suggest they may have some capacity for acclimatisation. However, the rate of change is likely to outpace natural adaptation for most species. I should mention that we're also looking at various mitigation strategies. These include reducing carbon emissions at their source, which remains the most effective approach, and exploring localised interventions such as protecting areas with naturally higher pH levels38. There are also emerging technologies being researched, though many remain experimental. In conclusion, ocean acidification represents one of the most significant threats to marine biodiversity in the coming decades. The science is clear, though uncertainty remains about the precise timeline and magnitude of impacts. What we do know is that action is needed at multiple levels, from individual behavioural changes to international policy agreements. For your next seminar, I'd like you to read the article by Doney and colleagues from 200939, which provides an excellent overview of the chemical processes involved. We'll also be visiting the marine research station next week40 for a practical demonstration of how scientists measure ocean pH in the field. Please ensure you've read the preparatory materials before we arrive. Are there any questions before we continue?
